claims.text: A hierarchical structure arranges the members of an organisation in levels, with each level answerable to the one above it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The span of control is the number of subordinates one manager or supervisor is directly responsible for.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The chain of command is the line of authority running from the top of the hierarchy to the bottom, along which instructions pass down and accountability passes back up.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A tall structure has many levels of hierarchy with narrow spans of control, while a short structure has few levels with wide spans; in a tall structure a decision passes through more levels, so decisions tend to be slower and messages can be distorted on the way down the chain of command.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The directors of a company are chosen by the shareholders to set its overall direction; they take the key long-term decisions and answer to the shareholders for the results.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Managers run a department or function within the direction the directors set; supervisors oversee day-to-day work at the first level above the operatives; other employees carry out the operational tasks of the business, from serving customers to packing orders.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Each level depends on the others: directors set objectives that managers turn into departmental targets, supervisors turn targets into daily instructions for other employees, and information about results travels back up the same chain.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The functions of management are planning, organising, coordinating, commanding and controlling.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Planning sets objectives and decides in advance how to reach them; organising arranges people, tasks and resources to carry the plan out; coordinating makes the separate parts work together; commanding directs and instructs staff; controlling checks actual results against the plan and corrects deviations.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Planning usually comes first among the functions, because the other functions need a plan to organise towards, coordinate around and check against.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Delegation is the passing of authority from a manager to a subordinate to carry out a task or take decisions, while the manager remains answerable for the outcome.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Delegation tends to lighten a manager's workload and develops the subordinate's skills and confidence, which can also raise motivation and prepare staff for greater responsibility.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Delegation carries risks: a subordinate may lack the skill the manager assumed, or errors may go unnoticed where the manager keeps no check, and the manager still answers for the results.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Trust and control are the two faces of delegation: trust gives the subordinate freedom over how the work is done, while control keeps the manager's check on progress and quality; effective delegation balances the two against the subordinate's experience and the importance of the task.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An autocratic leadership style is one in which the leader makes decisions alone and instructs staff what to do.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A democratic leadership style is one in which the leader consults the team and draws on its views before deciding, while a laissez-faire style leaves the team to decide and organise the work itself with minimal interference from the leader.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A leadership style tends to shape motivation: consulted staff often feel their views count and are more willing to commit to decisions, while closely instructed staff may follow orders yet offer fewer ideas.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A leadership style is appropriate when it fits the circumstances - the experience and skill of the team, the urgency of the task and the leader's own knowledge of the work - so that it achieves the task without damaging the team's willingness to work.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Recommending a style weighs speed against commitment: an autocratic decision can be quicker where time is short or safety is at stake, whereas democratic consultation tends to produce better-supported decisions where the team is experienced and time allows.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A justified recommendation names the style, ties it to the circumstances of the case, weighs the case against it, and states the conditions that would change the choice.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A trade union is an organisation of workers that aims to protect and improve its members' pay and working conditions, mainly by negotiating with employers on their behalf.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Union members act together through collective bargaining: pay and conditions are negotiated between the employer and the union for the members jointly, rather than worker by worker, and members may support agreed measures, including industrial action, where talks fail.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Union membership tends to strengthen employees' bargaining power on pay, conditions and safety; for the employer, a recognised union offers a single channel for negotiation, while higher wage costs and, where talks stall, the risk of industrial action are among the effects an employer weighs.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Democratic leadership and delegation are different ideas: democratic leadership is a leader's general way of reaching decisions by consulting the team before deciding, while delegation is the passing of authority over a defined task to a named subordinate, which a leader of any style can do.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Autocratic and democratic leaders both take the final decision; the styles differ in what comes before it, because an autocratic leader decides alone and instructs, while a democratic leader seeks and uses the team's views first.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
